title: Aho: the wave finds it is water
hookLine: in chapter two the student stops asking and starts exclaiming, and the king bows to himself
carry: every wave is water: the self in everything
tomorrow: Why test a king who says he's free?

cards: Aho. It's a Sanskrit cry of wonder, the sound someone makes when a thing turns out bigger than expected. It's how King Janaka opens the second chapter.
In the first, he asked his three questions and listened. Now the teacher falls silent and the student speaks, and he doesn't ask anything. He exclaims.
A few verses in, he does something that makes a first-time reader look twice. He bows to himself.

teach.b: Chapter two begins, in paraphrase: Aho, I am spotless, at peace, pure awareness, beyond nature. All this time I've been fooled by delusion. Then Janaka reaches for the sea.

teach.h: WAVES, FOAM AND BUBBLES ARE WATER.
teach.b: As waves and foam and bubbles are nothing other than water, so this whole world, flowing out of the Self, is nothing other than the Self. A wave can rise high or crash on the rocks; it never stops being water.
Advaita's name for that one water is Brahman: one reality, showing up as everything. Then the verses that make people sit up. Wonderful am I, Janaka says.
Namo mahyam. I remain, even when the whole world, from the creator down to a blade of grass, is destroyed.

On the surface that sounds like a king who's had too much praise. But the I in these verses isn't Janaka with a crown and a treasury. It's the awareness he was pointed to on the first day, the witness.
Bowing to that, he bows to what he takes to be in everything, the blade of grass included. It's one reason many Hindus explain the joined-palm namaste as a bow to the divine in the other person.
On this reading, the small I that wants credit is exactly what has dropped away. What's left can't be flattered; there's no one left to flatter. That's why the chapter sounds like joy, not vanity.
A man who thought he was a wave has just found out he's water. And he doesn't explain it. He sings.

how: In the Ashtavakra Gita, chapter two is Janaka's response, and students reading the text with a teacher often treat it as a picture of what the sage's teaching sounds like once it lands: wonder rather than argument.

o: a Sanskrit cry of wonder, like wow
a word of thanks said after a teacher speaks
a short sigh of sorrow at the end of a prayer

games.q: Janaka's cry of wonder — tap the pairs.

s: in chapter two, Janaka keeps asking more questions
he stops asking and starts exclaiming: aho, I am spotless, at peace, pure awareness.
namo mahyam, a salutation to the Self, not to the king with the crown.
the wave picture says the world is separate from the Self
as waves and foam are nothing other than water, the world is nothing other than the Self.

games.q: you're Janaka. the sage has pointed you to awareness, and it has landed. what do you do?
o: break into wonder, and bow to the Self.
go back to running the kingdom as before.
games.why: chapter two is Janaka's cry: aho, and namo mahyam, salutation to me, meaning the Self in everything.

practice: Watch thoughts and feelings rise and fall like waves: a plan, a memory, a flicker of worry. Don't calm them; just watch each one rise and sink back, and notice what they rise in, the awareness itself, the water under the waves.
If a wave seems big, let it be big; it's still water.

wordCard.voice: Aho. A Sanskrit cry of wonder. Janaka opens chapter two with it, after finding out that a wave he thought he was has always been water.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: aho, a cry of wonder or surprise. Janaka opens chapter two with it.
